segments.title: Why the treaty ratios felt unequal
segments.body: A criticism of the treaty ratios is that national tonnage allowances translate poorly into whole ships. Britain and the United States retain equal leading shares, with Japan held below them. Using fifteen ships for each leading power gives France and Italy five and a quarter ships apiece. The fractional remainder cannot be transferred to their cruiser allowances. This calculation introduces the objection that the settlement leaves participants dissatisfied with both fleet numbers and the ships they can build.

evidence.note: The ratio translated into whole-ship totals gives France and Italy fractional allowances, forming part of the criticism of the settlement.

segments.summary: The 5:5:3:1.75:1.75 capital-ship ratio is criticized for leaving France and Italy with fractional ship allowances and the larger powers dissatisfied.

segments.title: A 42,000-ton capital-ship ceiling
segments.body: The proposed 42,000-ton ceiling starts from ships already in service or under construction when the treaty was negotiated. Hood's listed standard displacement supplies the benchmark, while the cancelled South Dakota and Kii designs show the scale of contemporary capital-ship projects. The Hawkins-class cruiser precedent provides a comparison: the treaty rounded above that design to a 10,000-ton, 8-inch-gun limit. Applying the same approach to Hood would leave room for balanced capital ships. The 16-inch gun ceiling remains acceptable in the proposal because guns of that calibre were already in service. Furious's exceptional 18-inch armament is set aside as a precedent for ordinary battleships.

evidence.note: Acceptance of the 16-inch ceiling despite Furious's exceptional 18-inch armament.
Comparison of Hood, South Dakota and Kii with a 42,000-ton, 16-inch-gun limit.

segments.summary: Using Hood and contemporary uncompleted designs as the benchmark, the proposed treaty allows 42,000-ton standard-displacement capital ships with 16-inch guns.

segments.title: Why a stronger ratio could reduce insecurity
segments.body: The case for a 10:7 ratio is that Japan could feel more secure while the United States retained greater naval and industrial strength. American victory would remain the expected outcome, but Japan would have a stronger chance of resisting an attack by a larger power. Doubling the existing French and Italian shares gives 3.5 each; the proposed settlement rounds those shares up to four, allowing eight ships under the new totals. Controlled construction would let every signatory replace obsolete vessels and keep its shipbuilding industry active. The proposal does not assume that greater naval confidence would end Japanese aggression. Its narrower aim is to reduce insecurity and resentment over the treaty while preserving American superiority.

evidence.note: The proposed 10:7 ratio and rounded French and Italian shares seek to preserve respect and security through controlled construction.

segments.summary: The proposed 10:7 ratio aims to reduce Japanese insecurity while preserving American naval and industrial superiority.

segments.title: When impractical limits make evasion normal
segments.body: The criticism of the 35,000-ton ceiling is that it makes evasion a condition of building an adequate capital ship. Treating water as armour in the Nelson-class calculations is offered as a British example of working around the nominal limit. Once false declarations become routine, confidence in the remaining rules also erodes. This critique connects restrictions on new construction and upgrades with the wartime vulnerability of Hood, Prince of Wales, and Repulse. The wider objection concerns rules that cannot be enforced or obeyed without compromising the ships they govern.

evidence.note: Criticism of the tonnage ceiling through Nelson-class accounting, false declarations and limits on new designs and upgrades.

segments.summary: The 35,000-ton ceiling is criticized for encouraging creative accounting and dangerous design compromises.

segments.title: Replacement rules that keep shipyards working
segments.body: The alternative treaty permits each signatory to keep at most one fifth of its capital-ship tonnage under construction, with permission to build up to its fleet limit from 1922. Ships laid down before 1914 with guns of 14 inches or less become eligible for replacement in 1926; pre-1914 ships with larger guns follow in 1930. Ships laid down during 1914-1918 become eligible in 1934, and those laid down during 1919-1922 follow in 1936. Treaty-era ships must complete 18 years of service before replacement. This schedule would keep Japanese construction moving at roughly one ship a year, with some gaps. Even the proposed eight-ship French and Italian fleets could support nearly continuous work at one construction yard, with another yard maintaining the ships already in service. Predictable construction would also make each navy's replacement programme easier for the other signatories to monitor.

evidence.note: One-fifth construction ceiling, replacement eligibility in 1926, 1930, 1934 and 1936, and an 18-year service requirement for treaty-era ships.

segments.summary: The alternative treaty limits simultaneous construction and stages replacements by a ship's age instead of imposing a long building holiday.

segments.title: Fleet totals and national choices
segments.body: Britain and the United States receive capacity for twenty 42,000-ton ships, Japan fourteen, and France and Italy eight each under the proposed treaty. The American allowance is 840,000 tons, and the example includes completing Washington in 1922. Space within the fleet total does not mean all the corresponding ships can be built at once. The American example initially has room for six new ships, but the one-fifth construction ceiling limits simultaneous building to four at that size. Replacement eligibility later releases more tonnage as older ships leave service. Each navy can therefore plan a sequence of orders within both its total allowance and the separate construction limit.

evidence.note: The proposed national allowances, completion of Washington, and the distinction between available replacement tonnage and simultaneous construction.

segments.summary: Proposed fleet allowances create room for new capital ships, while the one-fifth construction ceiling limits how many can be built together.

segments.title: Smaller battleships for French and Italian fleets
segments.body: The proposed 42,000-ton ceiling would let smaller powers build below the maximum when their infrastructure or requirements favored a smaller ship. Dunkerque provides an example of a design kept below its treaty allowance because of infrastructure constraints. A proposed national allowance of 336,000 tons could support ten ships of 33,600 tons. That is close to the 33,800-ton figure cited for Nelson and Rodney. A smaller design might suit French or Italian requirements even if it was less suitable for a navy expected to fight worldwide.

evidence.note: Infrastructure constraints, the 336,000-ton allowance and ten 33,600-ton ships illustrate different national design requirements.

segments.summary: A maximum displacement leaves France and Italy free to choose smaller battleships and obtain more hulls within the proposed national allowance.

segments.title: Three British fleets and regional reinforcement
segments.body: Choosing 40,000-ton ships would let Britain fit twenty-one capital ships into the proposed 840,000-ton allowance. The suggested distribution places seven at Trincomalee, seven in the Mediterranean and seven with the Home Fleet. This falls below the preferred total of three eight-ship fleets but meets the stated minimum of seven per fleet. Against Japan, the Indian Ocean force could wait for Mediterranean reinforcements to bring its seven ships up to fourteen. The same ability to concentrate ships would affect comparisons with French or American forces in an individual theatre. Security in this arrangement depends on reinforcement between stations as well as national fleet totals.

evidence.note: Twenty-one British ships form three seven-ship fleets, with Mediterranean reinforcement changing local force ratios.

segments.summary: Twenty-one 40,000-ton ships would give Britain three seven-ship fleets, with Mediterranean reinforcements changing the balance in another theatre.

segments.title: Japanese security and the Yamato counterfactual
segments.body: The Japanese option assumes fourteen ships built to the full 42,000-ton standard limit. Britain and the United States might choose twenty-one smaller ships instead, leaving Japan with a 70-percent tonnage share but fewer hulls. In this counterfactual, Japanese planners could take confidence from the greater individual size of their ships while their opponents relied on additional numbers. Yamato and Musashi are interpreted as an overreaction to perceived battle-line weakness. Continued construction under a less restrictive ratio is therefore suggested as a possible reason Japan might not pursue those ships, without treating that outcome as certain.

evidence.note: The tentative Yamato and Musashi counterfactual connects perceived weakness with the alternative of fourteen larger Japanese ships against twenty-one smaller opponents.

segments.summary: A larger permitted Japanese fleet raises the possibility that perceived battle-line weakness would no longer drive a Yamato-scale response.

segments.title: Shipbuilding as interwar industrial policy
segments.body: The proposal accepts a slower pace of British debt repayment rather than a return to the pre-1914 dreadnought race. A steady capital-ship program would keep yards, suppliers, research, and design work active. That spending would also circulate through the economy, especially when governments confront a downturn. Construction limits therefore determine whether a state preserves the industrial capacity it may later need.

evidence.note: A modest continuing construction programme would slow debt repayment while sustaining shipbuilding research and industrial employment during economic downturns.

segments.summary: A controlled capital-ship program could preserve design skills, suppliers, and research while also supporting the wider economy during a downturn.

segments.title: A Royal Navy of early fast battleships
segments.body: The suggested Royal Navy programme starts with three batches of three ships before settling into smaller orders. Nine new ships would allow older 13.5-inch-gun vessels to retire after their replacements entered service. The proposed 40,000-ton ships would make 28 to 30 knots, carry nine 16-inch guns and retain substantial protection. All-forward armament follows the Nelson and Rodney layout to use displacement efficiently. Because battlecruisers would consume the same capital-ship allowance, fast battleships could provide speed while remaining suitable for the battle line. Continuous building would also preserve the construction industry. In this counterfactual, a modern British battle line would make Germany's new ships look less exceptional beside the Royal Navy.

evidence.note: British construction batches, 40,000-ton fast battleships, industrial continuity and the deterrent value of a modern battle line.

segments.summary: The British alternative centers on 40,000-ton fast battleships, replacing older ships steadily without exceeding the construction allowance.

segments.title: Why security matters to treaty enforcement
segments.body: The postwar 'never again' conviction encouraged negotiators to treat the removal of weapons as a direct route to peace. This critique asks how limits can survive when the signatories believe those limits leave them insecure. Voluntary compliance depends on their acceptance of the bargain, while enforcing a peace treaty through war contradicts its purpose. Britain faces imperial commitments with a reduced fleet, Japan regards its ratio as a political slight, and the United States retains a slow battle line. The American construction pause is also linked to weakened industrial capacity and an urgent rebuilding effort before 1941. Hawaii's shortage of reconnaissance aircraft provides a specific example of the resulting readiness concerns. The estimate gives reconnaissance coverage of only 60 degrees, compared with a full 360-degree search or at least roughly 240 degrees toward the expected threat.

evidence.note: Postwar disarmament aims, enforcement through consent or coercion, and the critique of national insecurity and American readiness.

segments.summary: The enforcement critique links voluntary compliance to national security concerns and questions the use of force to uphold a peace treaty.

segments.title: Modelling a Kii-based Japanese battleship
segments.body: Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts does not distinguish standard displacement from full load in this exercise. The Japanese model therefore receives a 47,000-ton allowance, representing the proposed 42,000-ton standard limit plus an assumed 5,000 tons of additional load. Its ten main guns retain the Kii-based arrangement, although four triple turrets are considered a possible alternative for greater firepower. The model substitutes eighteen 6-inch secondary guns for sixteen 5.5-inch guns, and its 16-inch main guns approximate Japanese 410 mm weapons. It also carries a quadruple torpedo launcher on each side. One in-game funnel complex provides sufficient efficiency, so a second funnel is omitted to avoid adding weight merely for appearance.

evidence.note: The Kii-based model's assumed load allowance, alternative turret arrangement, secondary-gun substitutions, torpedoes and funnel compromise.

segments.summary: The Kii-based model approximates a 42,000-ton standard-displacement ship with a 47,000-ton game allowance and explicit armament compromises.

segments.title: American firepower at the cost of speed
segments.body: The American South Dakota-derived model assumes 40,000 tons standard displacement, allowing a twenty-first ship within the proposed fleet allowance. Its 45,000-ton game target includes an assumed 5,000-ton load margin, although the finished model exceeds that target by 430 tons. The model carries twelve 16-inch guns and makes 23 knots, against 30 knots for the Japanese design. Increasing speed within this model would require sacrificing a turret. A British-style arrangement with all-forward armament is considered as another possible development if construction continued. The chosen American model retains the larger battery, accepting that the faster Japanese ships can disengage.

evidence.note: The South Dakota-derived model's 40,000-ton standard target, 45,000-ton game allowance, 430-ton excess and gun-versus-speed compromise.

segments.summary: The South Dakota-derived model trades speed for twelve 16-inch guns, while aiming at a smaller standard displacement than its Japanese opponent.

segments.title: Eighty-four guns against fifty in a 1926 scenario
segments.body: The game encounter places seven twelve-gun American battleships against five ten-gun Japanese ships. That gives the American force eighty-four 16-inch guns against fifty, or thirty-four additional shells in a full salvo. Keeping at long range would let the Japanese exploit their speed instead of closing directly against the larger battery. The recorded Japanese approach does not initially make full use of that advantage. The scenario is set in 1926 with visual aiming before radar, and a possible Japanese preference for a night action remains outside the daylight test.

evidence.note: The seven-against-five force comparison gives 84 versus 50 main guns, with Japanese speed, daylight conditions and 1926 visual aiming defining the game scenario.

segments.summary: Seven American ships bring eighty-four 16-inch guns against fifty Japanese guns in a daylight scenario using visual fire control.

segments.title: When gun counts become comparable
segments.body: Raw gun totals can mislead at Tsushima because the weapons and capabilities were not uniform. In the simulated encounter, both sides use 16-inch batteries and broadly comparable rangefinding technology. They also employ those weapons in similar ways. Under these assumptions, a larger volume of fire provides more opportunities to score hits. The comparison depends on that technical similarity, so the same reasoning cannot simply be transferred to fleets with substantially different guns.

evidence.note: Comparison of misleading raw gun counts at Tsushima with comparable 16-inch batteries and rangefinding in the simulation.

segments.summary: The simulation makes raw gun totals more informative than at Tsushima because both fleets use comparable weapons and rangefinding systems.

segments.title: The Eight-Eight Plan and fast-battleship logic
segments.body: Japan's Eight-Eight Fleet Plan called for eight battleships and eight battlecruisers. The case for a separate battlecruiser force weakened when Japan could reach an opponent's distant trade routes only after defeating its battle fleet. Commerce raiding therefore offered less immediate value than an advantage in the main fleet action. Fast battleships could give the Japanese battle line greater speed than its opponents while serving that central purpose.

evidence.note: The Eight-Eight Fleet Plan and the need to defeat enemy battle fleets before reaching distant commerce support the case for fast battleships.

segments.summary: Japan's need to defeat enemy battle fleets before reaching distant trade routes strengthens the case for fast battleships.

segments.title: Carrier scouting for a slow American battle line
segments.body: The Japanese ships use their speed to disappear from the simulated American force. A 23-knot battle line would struggle to catch them without other means of finding and following the enemy. The American doctrinal explanation assigns carriers the scouting role associated with the Lexington battlecruisers. Once the enemy is located, the battle fleet can continue advancing until the opponent can no longer avoid engagement. Scouting therefore forms an essential part of the proposed use of the slower battleships.

evidence.note: Japanese disengagement and the carrier scouting role that supports a slower American battle line.

segments.summary: Carriers inherit the Lexington battlecruisers' scouting role in an American approach that accepts a slower battle line.

segments.title: Armour schemes and intended fighting range
segments.body: The Kii-derived ship carries roughly 11 to 12 inches of belt armour, compared with about 13.5 inches on the South Dakota derivative. The thinner Japanese belt assumes fighting near maximum range, where opposing shells should struggle to penetrate it. The thicker American belt permits a closer engagement. Those figures also support the argument for treating Hood as a fast battleship when comparing its protection with the Kii proposal.

evidence.note: The Kii and South Dakota belt figures imply different fighting ranges and support the argument for classifying Hood as a fast battleship.

segments.summary: The Kii- and South Dakota-derived armour schemes express different tactical assumptions about speed, range, and acceptable exposure.

segments.title: Using speed to divide a stronger battle line
segments.body: One proposed Japanese tactic is to split the squadron and approach the American battle line from several directions. This would use the speed advantage to divide American fire. The simulation instead keeps the five Japanese ships together. Concentration is understandable when their fifty main guns face eighty-four, so splitting the force remains an untested tactical alternative.

evidence.note: A proposed use of Japanese speed to divide American fire is balanced against the smaller squadron's reason to remain together.

segments.summary: Splitting the faster Japanese squadron could divide American fire, although the smaller force also has reasons to remain concentrated.

segments.title: A cap arms-control advocates could defend
segments.body: The proposal rejects a 45,000-ton ceiling because it would permit ships larger than Hood and appear to give naval expansion too much room. A 42,000-ton ceiling could be presented to disarmament advocates as a limit around the largest ship already in service. Naval constructors would still have room to develop more efficient designs within it. Britain might choose 40,000-ton ships to obtain an extra hull, while American and Japanese choices remain uncertain. For the American model, an additional 2,000 tons would be assigned to speed, although the resulting gain is not calculated.

evidence.note: Comparison of 42,000 and 45,000 tons as politically different bargains for naval and peace constituencies.

segments.summary: The proposed 42,000-ton ceiling uses Hood as a bargaining reference, while an extra 2,000 tons on the American model would be reserved for speed.

segments.title: Why the bare battle-line test is artificial
segments.body: The speed gap lets the Japanese force choose whether to close, so the simplified experiment makes the Americans look tactically constrained. A real US fleet would include fast cruisers and destroyers in large numbers. Those screening forces mean seven battleships would not normally meet five opponents as an isolated battle line. The scenario is a controlled comparison of design tradeoffs rather than a prediction of a historical fleet action.

evidence.note: Japanese speed controls contact in the simplified encounter, but American fast cruisers and destroyers make an isolated battle-line action unrealistic.

segments.summary: The isolated battleship encounter is a controlled design comparison, not a forecast of how complete American and Japanese fleets would fight.

segments.title: Range, speed, and American machinery
segments.body: The notional American ship's 23-knot speed forms part of a wider machinery tradeoff. American ships needed to travel long distances, and an engine suited to steady cruising did not automatically deliver high maximum speed efficiently. Long-distance cruising and high-speed operation place competing demands on turbine and engine design. Separate turbines for cruising and high-speed operation offer one way to reconcile them. Such an arrangement depends on turbine efficiency being sufficiently developed to make it useful.

evidence.note: The conflict between long-range cruising efficiency and high speed in turbine design.

segments.summary: The American emphasis on long-distance steaming helps explain why extracting more speed from battleship machinery was not a simple design choice.

segments.title: Ammunition exhaustion and the model's torpedo imbalance
segments.body: Ammunition exhaustion raises a further limitation of the simulated comparison. Both designs carry 6-inch secondary guns, but the Japanese ships also have torpedo launchers. The American model omits the proposed single-torpedo fittings because they seemed of little use against a Japanese broadside of four torpedoes. That omission is then reconsidered as a possible strategic mistake. The concern remains a forecast about the model, since the fleets have not yet exhausted their ammunition.

evidence.note: The possible consequences of ammunition exhaustion draw attention to Japanese torpedoes and omitted American torpedo fittings.

segments.summary: The Japanese model retains torpedoes that the American design omits, a difference that could matter after the heavy guns exhaust their ammunition.

segments.title: What the simulated fleet action shows
segments.body: The recorded simulation does not show a decisive victory before it is saved and stopped. The American ships withstand their larger Japanese opponents, while superior American numbers and gunfire fail to overwhelm the faster force. Both squadrons remain sufficiently concentrated to preserve their firepower and avoid being divided. Severe damage, ammunition exhaustion and an inconclusive return are the expected ending, rather than a completed result shown in the recording. Cruisers and destroyers are identified as possible deciding forces in a fuller fleet action. The first of four runs was selected for the video.

evidence.note: Neither the American numerical advantage nor the larger Japanese design produces an easy victory, and cruisers or destroyers could affect a fuller action.
Ammunition exhaustion and an inconclusive return with severe damage are forecasts, not a completed battle outcome.
The fleets maintain concentration and avoid being divided despite erratic game manoeuvres.
The battle is saved and stopped, followed by the explanation that the first of four runs was selected.

segments.summary: The recorded American-Japanese encounter remains undecided, illustrating design tradeoffs while leaving its eventual outcome unobserved.

segments.title: How the British design changes the comparison
segments.body: The hypothetical British ships exchange some American firepower for greater speed. Seven ships with nine guns each would bring sixty-three heavy guns against the Japanese force's fifty. Their proposed 28-knot speed would leave only a two-knot disadvantage, making Japanese disengagement more difficult than against the slower American model. Greater British protection would also change the balance. The Japanese model's 30-knot speed is itself a rounded approximation of 29.75 knots. These calculations motivate a further comparison that has not been demonstrated by the battle shown.

evidence.note: A proposed British-Japanese comparison uses 63 versus 50 guns and 28 versus 30 knots, with Japanese speed rounded from 29.75 knots.

segments.summary: A proposed British comparison substitutes nine-gun fast battleships for the slower twelve-gun American ships.

segments.title: A workable ceiling rewards naval constructors
segments.body: The proposed 40,000- to 42,000-ton range is intended to let each signatory build a credible capital ship. A common ceiling would prevent a navy from compensating for inefficient design simply by adding displacement. Competition would instead depend on naval constructors, shipyards and how effectively they used the available tonnage. In this proposal, the higher allowance removes the design constraints criticized at 35,000 tons while retaining a limit on ship size. That is the intended reason for signatories to regard compliance as workable.

evidence.note: A workable common ceiling would make design efficiency and shipyard capability matter while limiting displacement increases.

segments.summary: The proposed common ceiling would shift competition toward naval constructors, shipyards and efficient use of the permitted displacement.

segments.title: Why one extra battleship changes American basing
segments.body: Within the proposed tonnage allowance, 40,000-ton ships could give the United States twenty-one battleships instead of twenty. The twenty-ship alternative suggests five four-ship divisions, with three in the Pacific and two in the Atlantic. Twenty-one ships instead allow six three-ship divisions and three flagships, forming seven-ship squadrons at Hawaii, San Diego and on the Atlantic coast. Fourteen ships would then be available in the Pacific, matching the hypothetical Japanese fleet, while seven faced Britain's Atlantic force. A twenty-ship fleet could use a similar distribution, but one squadron would have only six ships. The extra hull changes the local numerical balance without increasing the national tonnage allowance.

evidence.note: Twenty versus twenty-one American ships permit different divisional structures and regional deployments within the same tonnage.

segments.summary: Twenty-one American battleships allow three seven-ship squadrons and a different regional balance from a fleet of twenty.

segments.title: What 252 guns against 140 means per salvo
segments.body: Twenty-one twelve-gun American ships would carry 252 main guns, while fourteen ten-gun Japanese ships would carry 140. That gives the American fleet 112 additional shells in a full salvo. At an assumed five-percent hit rate, the calculation yields roughly twelve or thirteen American hits against seven Japanese hits. These are illustrative figures for comparable 16-inch batteries. The assumed hit rate is separate from any accuracy observed in the game.

evidence.note: Full-fleet gun counts and a hypothetical five-percent hit rate illustrate the potential American salvo advantage.

segments.summary: Scaling the hypothetical fleets to twenty-one American and fourteen Japanese ships gives 252 main guns against 140.

segments.title: How radar changes high-speed approaches
segments.body: Radar-controlled gunnery changes the tactical value of high-speed approaches. Detection beyond gun range can provide time to prepare a firing solution before an opponent closes. Visual confirmation may follow in daylight, while a night engagement can proceed without it. North Cape and Admiral Lee illustrate another choice: withholding fire until close range so that the opening salvos cause heavy damage.

evidence.note: Radar detection, firing-solution preparation, daylight or night engagement, and close-range opening salvos, with North Cape and Admiral Lee as named examples.

segments.summary: Radar detection and prepared firing solutions change the risks of using speed to move into and out of contact.

segments.title: Credible limits and continued modernization
segments.body: The deterrence argument accepts disarmament as a sincere response to war's destruction but disputes the expectation that weakness can preserve peace. The maxim si vis pacem, para bellum expresses the alternative: preparing to resist an attack can help prevent one. A schoolyard analogy uses the appearance of strength to explain why a bully may avoid a target without a fight taking place. That analogy concerns governments' conduct rather than an inherent national character. Its application to the treaty is that signatories should retain enough capability to feel secure, with a 42,000-ton ceiling still giving disarmament advocates a limit they could defend.

evidence.note: Si vis pacem, para bellum and the schoolyard analogy support the case for deterrence through the appearance of strength.

segments.summary: The case for deterrence through perceived strength uses a schoolyard analogy to explain why an apparently capable opponent may discourage aggression.

segments.title: A forward fleet needs a functioning base
segments.body: Merely moving the Pacific Fleet to Hawaii does not make it a deterrent. Admirals James O. Richardson and Husband E. Kimmel argued that the deployment needed supplies, protection, reconnaissance assets, and a proper base. With that support, Hawaii becomes a credible forward position; without it, the concentration of ships can advertise vulnerability. The example leads back to treaty design, since a navy denied the forces it believes necessary may act from fear and insecurity. Perceived strength shapes both an opponent's calculation and a state's confidence in the agreement.

evidence.note: Admirals Richardson and Kimmel argued that a Hawaii base needed supplies, protection, and reconnaissance to support deterrence and national confidence.

segments.summary: Admirals James O. Richardson and Husband E. Kimmel illustrate why moving the Pacific Fleet to Hawaii could signal weakness unless reconnaissance, protection, logistics, and other support followed.

segments.title: Non-proliferation and the cost of blanket prohibition
segments.body: The nuclear-policy analogy combines support for non-proliferation treaties with criticism of restrictions on sharing civilian research. It distinguishes reactors intended to produce weapons material from designs for power generation. The counterfactual claim is that wider civilian cooperation could have provided nuclear electricity for decades and reduced dependence on imported fossil fuels. Solar and wind power are welcomed, but the objection concerns the earlier decades when nuclear generation could already have been available. Countries with large hydroelectric installations provide a comparison for the energy-security benefits claimed. This is an argument about the consequences of broad restrictions, rather than a technical assessment of individual reactor designs.

evidence.note: The nuclear-policy analogy supports non-proliferation while criticizing restrictions on civilian research and arguing for energy-security benefits from nuclear and hydroelectric power.

segments.summary: A modern non-proliferation analogy asks how arms control can restrict weapons while still sharing civilian technology and preserving security.

segments.title: Continuous construction and equitable outcomes
segments.body: Halting capital-ship construction threatens the industry that builds those ships unless the government buys and maintains the idle infrastructure. Losing that capacity would make a later restart more difficult. In the British example, initial batches give way to two new capital ships every two years, with no more than four under construction at once. America could follow a comparable rhythm, while Japan could replace older ships in pairs as eligibility dates arrived. The American example also permits completing Washington, although that remains a national choice. The intended outcome is proportionate value for each signatory, allowing different fleets while preserving the ability to replace ships.

evidence.note: Idle capital-ship infrastructure would need government purchase and maintenance to survive a construction halt, or become harder to rebuild later.
British, American and Japanese replacement rhythms illustrate treaty benefits proportionate to each navy's requirements.

segments.summary: The proposed replacement rhythm aims to preserve shipbuilding capacity and give each navy a proportionate reason to accept the settlement.

segments.title: How capital-ship limits spill into cruiser evasion
segments.body: The critique of the treaty series links increasingly restrictive limits with creative displacement declarations. Japanese cruisers face additional pressure because they must help compensate for a battle line that cannot receive new battleships. Under the proposed settlement, credible new battleships would reduce that burden on cruisers. The forecast still expects Japanese ships nominally limited to 42,000 tons to reach perhaps 43,000 or 44,000 tons. Its claimed benefit is reduced pressure for cruiser evasion, rather than the disappearance of misstatement. A treaty that permits useful construction would also give Japan a reason to keep other signatories within the same restrictions.

evidence.note: New battleships could reduce Japanese pressure to misstate cruiser displacement, even while nominally 42,000-ton battleships might exceed that limit.

segments.summary: New Japanese battleships could reduce the pressure to overload cruisers, although the counterfactual still anticipates displacement misstatements.

segments.title: A negotiating victory too complete to last
segments.body: The negotiators' desire to prevent another war is treated as sincere in this critique. The objection is that persuasive rhetoric and intelligence advantages secured terms too restrictive for the naval powers to sustain. Routine false declarations would undermine confidence in the remaining rules. Sovereign states could accept enforcement voluntarily, but imposing the agreement through war would contradict its stated purpose. British use of the treaty's wording and advantages in the later London agreements are presented as responses that leave the original problems unresolved. The proposed alternative bases peace on states retaining enough capability to feel secure and respect one another's strength.

evidence.note: The critique links restrictive disarmament terms to routine evasion, limits on enforcement and unresolved problems in the London treaties.

segments.summary: In this critique, disarmament terms that require routine evasion undermine confidence in the agreement and leave enforcement dependent on consent or force.
